title: Introduction to Mechanical Engineering

sources.title: UCL Module Catalogue 2026/27: MECH0003 Introduction to Mechanical Engineering
sources.used_for: aims, ordered topic list (thermofluids then statics), learning outcomes, credits, term and assessment

about: MECH0003 is a 15-credit Term 1 module in UCL Mechanical Engineering made up of two strands: Thermofluids (systems and control volumes, pressure and hydrostatic head, mass and energy balances, and the First Law with flow) and Applied Mechanics: Statics (forces and moments, rigid body equilibrium, friction, structures, distributed forces and internal forces). Its learning outcomes include applying these ideas to an engine and a bridge-like structure and analysing experimental results. According to the 2026/27 UCL module catalogue it is assessed by an exam (60%), two in-class activities (20%) and two pieces of coursework (20%).
topics: Introduction to thermodynamics and fluid concepts
Analysing systems; pressure and hydrostatic head
Mass balance, isothermal flow and flow analysis
Energy conservation and the First Law for closed systems
The First Law with flow and its applications
Analysis of structures: trusses and frames
Distributed forces and centre of gravity
Internal forces and moments in structures

notes.body:
Thermofluids combines thermodynamics (energy, heat and work) with fluid mechanics (how liquids and gases move and exert forces). The first step in any problem is to define precisely what you are analysing.

Systems:
- Closed system (control mass): a fixed quantity of matter; energy can cross the boundary as heat or work, but mass cannot. Example: gas in a sealed piston–cylinder.
- Open system (control volume): a region in space through which mass flows. Example: a pump, turbine, nozzle or length of pipe.
- Isolated system: neither mass nor energy crosses the boundary.
- The boundary can be real or imaginary, fixed or moving.

Properties and state:
- A property is any measurable characteristic of the system's state: pressure p, temperature T, volume V, mass m, internal energy U.
- Intensive properties do not depend on the amount of matter (p, T, density ρ); extensive properties do (V, m, U). Dividing an extensive property by mass gives a specific property, for example specific volume v = V/m = 1/ρ.
- A state is fixed by a small number of independent properties (two for a simple compressible substance of fixed composition).
- A process is a change of state; a cycle returns the system to its initial state.
- Equilibrium: properties are uniform and unchanging; a quasi-static process passes through a sequence of equilibrium states.

Temperature and the zeroth law: if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This is the basis of thermometry. Absolute temperature T (K) = θ (°C) + 273.15; always use kelvin in thermodynamic equations.

Ideal gas model: pV = mRT or pv = RT, where R is the specific gas constant: R = R̄/M with R̄ = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K). For air, R ≈ 0.287 kJ/(kg·K). Example: air at 100 kPa and 300 K has ρ = p/(RT) = 100 000/(287 × 300) ≈ 1.16 kg/m³.

What makes a fluid a fluid:
- A fluid deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small; a solid resists shear with a finite deformation.
- Viscosity μ relates shear stress to rate of shear strain: τ = μ du/dy for a Newtonian fluid. Water at room temperature has μ of about 1 × 10⁻³ Pa·s.
- No-slip condition: fluid in contact with a solid wall moves with the wall.
- Continuum assumption: properties are treated as smooth functions of position, valid when the scale of interest is much larger than molecular spacing.
- Liquids are usually treated as incompressible; gases are compressible, although gas flows at low Mach number (below about 0.3) can often be treated as incompressible.

Units: work in SI units throughout (Pa, J, kg, m, s, K) and be careful with kPa and kJ. 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa = 100 kPa.

Exam tips: start every answer by sketching the system or control volume, marking its boundary and what crosses it, and listing assumptions (steady, ideal gas, negligible kinetic energy, and so on).

Pressure is the normal force per unit area exerted by a fluid: p = F/A, measured in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). In a fluid at rest, pressure at a point acts equally in all directions.

Absolute and gauge pressure:
- Absolute pressure is measured from a perfect vacuum.
- Gauge pressure is measured relative to local atmospheric pressure: p_gauge = p_abs − p_atm. Standard atmospheric pressure is 101.325 kPa.
- Thermodynamic equations (such as pv = RT) always need absolute pressure.

Hydrostatics: in a fluid at rest, pressure increases with depth. For a fluid of constant density:
p = p₀ + ρgh
where h is the depth below the free surface where the pressure is p₀. This follows from vertical force balance on a small fluid element: dp/dz = −ρg, with z measured upwards.
- Pressure depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container (the 'hydrostatic paradox').
- Points at the same level in a continuous body of the same fluid at rest are at the same pressure.

Pressure head: h = p/(ρg) expresses a pressure as the height of a column of fluid that would produce it. This is the language of pumps and pipe systems.

Worked example: at 10 m depth in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²):
- p_gauge = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98.1 kPa.
- p_abs = 98.1 + 101.3 ≈ 199.4 kPa, roughly two atmospheres.

Manometers: use the rule that pressure is equal at the same level in the same continuous fluid, then add ρgh going down and subtract going up.
- U-tube with mercury (relative density 13.6) measuring a gas pressure difference with a 200 mm level difference: Δp = 13 600 × 9.81 × 0.2 ≈ 26.7 kPa (the gas's own weight is negligible).
- If the fluid above the mercury is water, use the density difference: Δp = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.2 ≈ 24.7 kPa.

Forces on submerged plane surfaces:
- Resultant force F = ρ g h_c A, where h_c is the depth of the centroid of the area.
- It acts at the centre of pressure, below the centroid: h_cp = h_c + I_G/(h_c A), where I_G is the second moment of area about the horizontal axis through the centroid.
- Example: a vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high with its top at the water surface. h_c = 1.5 m and A = 6 m², so F = 1000 × 9.81 × 1.5 × 6 ≈ 88.3 kN. I_G = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴, so h_cp = 1.5 + 4.5/(1.5 × 6) = 2.0 m below the surface, two-thirds of the depth, as expected for a triangular pressure distribution starting at zero.

Buoyancy (Archimedes): the upward force on a submerged body equals the weight of fluid displaced, ρ_fluid g V_displaced.

Exam tips: say whether pressures are gauge or absolute, label the levels in manometer problems, and remember that the resultant force acts at the centre of pressure, not the centroid.

notes.h: Mass balance, isothermal flow and flow analysis
notes.body:
Conservation of mass is the first equation for any flow problem.

Mass balance for a control volume:
dm_CV/dt = Σṁ_in − Σṁ_out
- At steady state, nothing in the control volume changes with time, so Σṁ_in = Σṁ_out.
- Mass flow rate ṁ = ρAV, where V is the mean velocity normal to the area A. Volume flow rate Q = AV.
- For an incompressible fluid in a pipe: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ (continuity), so the velocity rises where the pipe narrows.

Worked example: water flows at 2 m/s in a 100 mm diameter pipe that reduces to 50 mm.
- Q = (π/4) × 0.1² × 2 = 0.0157 m³/s, so ṁ = 15.7 kg/s.
- Halving the diameter quarters the area, so V₂ = 2 × 4 = 8 m/s.

Unsteady example (tank): if 5 kg/s of water flows into a tank and 3 kg/s flows out, the stored mass increases at 2 kg/s; with a tank plan area of 0.5 m², the level rises at 2/(1000 × 0.5) = 0.004 m/s.

Mechanical energy in isothermal flow: when there is no heat transfer, no shaft work and no friction to turn mechanical energy into internal energy, the temperature stays constant and energy conservation reduces to a balance of pressure, kinetic and potential energy. For flow that is steady, incompressible and inviscid (frictionless), along a streamline, Bernoulli's equation holds:
p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant
or, in head form, p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = constant (pressure head + velocity head + elevation head).
All four conditions must hold; Bernoulli does not apply across a pump or turbine, or where friction losses are significant, unless extra terms are added.

Applying Bernoulli to the pipe above (horizontal, losses neglected): p₁ − p₂ = ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = ½ × 1000 × (64 − 4) = 30 kPa. This pressure drop at a contraction is the principle of the Venturi meter.

Real flows: add a head loss h_L for friction and fittings, and a pump head h_p where work is added:
p₁/(ρg) + V₁²/(2g) + z₁ + h_p = p₂/(ρg) + V₂²/(2g) + z₂ + h_L

Other applications:
- Free jet from a tank (Torricelli): V = √(2gh), ignoring losses. With h = 5 m, V ≈ 9.9 m/s.
- Pitot tube: measures stagnation pressure; V = √(2(p₀ − p)/ρ).

Dimensionless groups and model testing: the Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ compares inertial and viscous forces. In pipes, flow is typically laminar below about Re ≈ 2000–2300 and turbulent at higher values. For a scale model to behave like the full-size device (dynamic similarity), the relevant dimensionless groups, such as Re, must match; this is why model tests often need different speeds or fluids.

Exam tips: state the Bernoulli conditions every time you use it, choose points 1 and 2 where you know the most, and use continuity to link the velocities.

notes.h: Energy conservation and the First Law for closed systems
notes.body:
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only change form or cross a boundary. For thermodynamics, energy crosses the boundary of a closed system in two ways: heat and work.

Definitions:
- Heat Q: energy transfer caused by a temperature difference.
- Work W: energy transfer by any other means (a moving boundary, a rotating shaft, electrical work).
- Heat and work are not properties: they depend on the path of the process, not just the end states. Internal energy U is a property.

Sign convention used here: heat supplied to the system is positive, and work done by the system is positive. Then the First Law for a closed system is:
Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE
and usually ΔKE and ΔPE are negligible, giving Q − W = ΔU. (Some textbooks, and the IUPAC convention used in chemistry, take work done on the system as positive and write Q + W = ΔU. Always state your convention.)

For a cycle, ΔU = 0, so the net heat supplied equals the net work output: ∮δQ = ∮δW.

Boundary (displacement) work for a quasi-static process: W = ∫p dV, the area under the process on a p–V diagram.
- Constant volume: W = 0.
- Constant pressure: W = p(V₂ − V₁).
- Isothermal ideal gas: W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁).
- Polytropic process pVⁿ = constant (n ≠ 1): W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1).

Ideal gas internal energy and enthalpy: for an ideal gas u depends only on T: Δu = c_v ΔT and Δh = c_p ΔT, with c_p − c_v = R and γ = c_p/c_v. For air, approximately c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), c_v = 0.718 kJ/(kg·K), R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), γ = 1.4.

Worked example: 0.5 kg of air is heated from 300 K to 400 K.
- At constant volume: W = 0, so Q = ΔU = 0.5 × 0.718 × 100 = 35.9 kJ.
- At constant pressure: W = mRΔT = 0.5 × 0.287 × 100 = 14.35 kJ and ΔU = 35.9 kJ again (same temperature change), so Q = 35.9 + 14.35 = 50.25 kJ, which equals mc_pΔT. Heating at constant pressure needs more heat because some energy leaves as work.

Isothermal expansion of the same 0.5 kg of air at 300 K to double its volume: W = 0.5 × 0.287 × 300 × ln 2 ≈ 29.8 kJ. Since T is constant, ΔU = 0, so Q = W = 29.8 kJ.

Other forms of energy transfer: shaft work (W = Tω × time for a constant torque T and angular speed ω), electrical work (W = VIt), and stirring (paddle) work, which is always work done on the system.

Exam tips: draw the system boundary, state the sign convention, list what is zero (for example W = 0 in a rigid tank), and check units (kJ, not J mixed with kJ).

notes.h: The First Law with flow (steady-flow energy equation)
notes.body:
Most engineering devices (pumps, turbines, compressors, nozzles, heat exchangers) are open systems with fluid flowing through them. Energy is carried in and out with the mass as well as crossing the boundary as heat and work.

Flow work: pushing fluid into or out of a control volume requires work pv per unit mass. Combining it with internal energy gives the enthalpy, h = u + pv, which is why enthalpy appears in flow equations.

Steady-flow energy equation (SFEE) for one inlet (1) and one outlet (2), with heat into and work out of the control volume positive:
Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h₂ − h₁) + (V₂² − V₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)]
Assumptions: steady state (no accumulation of mass or energy), uniform properties at each inlet and outlet. Check units: h in J/kg when V²/2 is in m²/s² (= J/kg).

Standard simplifications:
- Turbine: usually adiabatic, ΔKE and ΔPE small: Ẇ = ṁ(h₁ − h₂), positive power output.
- Compressor or pump: adiabatic, Ẇ = ṁ(h₁ − h₂), negative, so power is input.
- Nozzle: no work, usually adiabatic; enthalpy is converted into kinetic energy: V₂² = V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂).
- Diffuser: the reverse of a nozzle.
- Throttling valve: no work, adiabatic, small ΔKE, so h₂ = h₁. For an ideal gas the temperature then stays constant.
- Heat exchanger: no work; heat lost by one stream equals heat gained by the other if the outside is adiabatic.
- Liquid pump (incompressible): ideal work per unit mass = vΔp = Δp/ρ, so power = QΔp. Pumping 0.01 m³/s of water through a 500 kPa rise needs at least 0.01 × 500 000 = 5 kW.

Worked example (compressor): air enters an adiabatic compressor at 300 K and leaves at 450 K, with ṁ = 0.5 kg/s. Treating air as an ideal gas with c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K) and neglecting KE and PE:
- Ẇ = ṁ c_p (T₁ − T₂) = 0.5 × 1.005 × (300 − 450) = −75.4 kW.
- The negative sign means 75.4 kW of power must be supplied.

Worked example (nozzle): air enters an adiabatic nozzle at 500 K and 10 m/s and leaves at 450 K.
- V₂ = √(V₁² + 2c_p(T₁ − T₂)) = √(10² + 2 × 1005 × 50) ≈ 317 m/s. Note c_p in J/(kg·K) here.

Mass balance for multiple streams: Σṁ_in = Σṁ_out; energy terms are summed over all inlets and outlets. For a mixing chamber with no heat or work, ṁ₁h₁ + ṁ₂h₂ = ṁ₃h₃.

Engines: the module's learning outcomes include using control volume analysis to understand the practical operation of an engine. Treat the whole engine as a control volume: fuel and air in, exhaust out, shaft work out and heat lost to the coolant and surroundings. The fraction of fuel energy turned into shaft work is the thermal efficiency.

Exam tips: sketch the control volume, list what is zero, keep kJ and J consistent (especially when kinetic energy is involved), and interpret the sign of your answer.

Statics deals with bodies at rest (or moving at constant velocity) under the action of forces. Forces are vectors: they have magnitude, direction and a line of action.

Resolving forces:
- In 2D, a force F at angle θ to the x-axis has components Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ.
- The resultant of several forces is found by adding components: R_x = ΣFx, R_y = ΣFy, R = √(R_x² + R_y²), direction tan α = R_y/R_x.
- Example: 3 kN east and 4 kN north combine to 5 kN at 53.1° north of east.
- In 3D, use unit vectors i, j, k; F = F_x i + F_y j + F_z k, with direction cosines.

Moment of a force about a point: M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action of the force. Units: N·m. Convention: anticlockwise positive in 2D (state your choice).
- Vector form: M = r × F, where r runs from the point to any point on the line of action. In 2D, M_z = x F_y − y F_x.
- Varignon's theorem: the moment of a force equals the sum of the moments of its components. Often it is easier to resolve first and then take moments of each component.

Worked example: a 500 N force is applied at the end of a 0.4 m spanner, at 30° to the line of the spanner. Only the component perpendicular to the spanner, 500 sin 30° = 250 N, has a lever arm (0.4 m); the component along the spanner passes through the bolt. M = 250 × 0.4 = 100 N·m.

Couples: two equal, opposite, parallel forces separated by a distance d form a couple of moment Fd. A couple has zero resultant force, and its moment is the same about every point (it is a free vector).

Equivalent systems: any force can be moved to a new point if a couple equal to its moment about the new point is added. Any system of forces in 2D can be reduced to a single resultant force and a couple at a chosen point, or to a single force with a particular line of action. This is how we find where a resultant acts.

Moment about an axis (3D): the component of r × F along the axis; used for shafts and hinges.

Typical pitfalls:
- Using the full force instead of its perpendicular component.
- Measuring the lever arm to the point of application rather than perpendicular to the line of action.
- Mixing clockwise and anticlockwise without a stated convention.

Exam tips: draw the force with its line of action extended, mark the perpendicular distance, and show components when the geometry is awkward.

A rigid body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant moment on it are both zero.

Equations of equilibrium:
- 2D: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM_O = 0 (about any point O). Three independent equations, so at most three unknowns can be found for a single body.
- 3D: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 as vectors, giving six scalar equations.
- Alternative 2D sets: two moment equations and one force equation, or three moment equations about non-collinear points.

Supports and their reactions (2D):
- Roller or smooth surface: one force normal to the surface.
- Cable or link: one force along the cable (tension only for a cable).
- Pin (hinge): two force components.
- Fixed support: two force components and a moment.
Each support prevents certain movements, and a reaction exists in each direction that is prevented.

The free body diagram (FBD) is essential:
1. Isolate the body by drawing it separately.
2. Show all external forces: applied loads, weights at the centre of gravity and reactions at every support or contact.
3. Mark dimensions and angles.
4. Choose axes and a moment convention.
Unknown reactions may be drawn in any direction; a negative result just means the real direction is opposite.

Two-force and three-force members:
- A two-force member (forces at only two points, no moments) is in equilibrium only if the two forces are equal, opposite and collinear along the line joining the points. Links and truss members are examples.
- A three-force member: the three forces must be concurrent (meet at a point) or parallel. This gives a quick graphical check.

Worked example: a horizontal beam AB, 4 m long, is pinned to a wall at A and held at B by a cable to the wall above A, making 30° with the beam. A 10 kN load hangs at B and the beam's weight is 2 kN at mid-length.
- Moments about A (the pin's unknowns drop out): T sin 30° × 4 = 10 × 4 + 2 × 2 = 44, so T = 22 kN.
- Horizontal: A_x = T cos 30° = 19.1 kN (the wall pushes the beam outwards, balancing the cable's inward pull).
- Vertical: A_y + T sin 30° = 12, so A_y = 12 − 11 = 1 kN upwards.
- Without the beam's weight, T = 20 kN and A_y = 0, a neat check.

Statical determinacy: if the supports provide exactly three independent reactions (for a 2D body) arranged so that they are neither all parallel nor all concurrent, the body is statically determinate and properly constrained. More reactions make it indeterminate; fewer, or badly arranged ones, leave it free to move.

The module applies these ideas to the bridge-like structures tested in the lab and to components under simple loads.

Exam tips: take moments about the point where the most unknowns act, write each equation with a label (ΣFx = 0), and finish with a check equation.

Friction is the tangential force at a contact that resists relative sliding. Dry (Coulomb) friction obeys simple empirical laws.

Coulomb friction model:
- Static friction can take any value up to a limit: F ≤ μ_s N, where N is the normal reaction and μ_s the coefficient of static friction.
- At impending motion (on the point of slipping): F = μ_s N.
- Once sliding: F = μ_k N, with μ_k (kinetic) usually a little smaller than μ_s.
- Friction acts on each body in the direction that opposes the relative motion (or tendency to move) of that body.
- In this model, friction is independent of the apparent contact area and of sliding speed.

Angle of friction: the resultant of N and F at impending slip makes an angle φ with the normal, where tan φ = μ_s. A block on an incline is on the point of sliding under its own weight when the incline angle equals φ.

Solving friction problems:
1. Draw the FBD with the friction force in the direction that opposes the tendency to move.
2. Decide whether you know the state: if the problem says 'about to slip', use F = μN.
3. If you do not know, assume equilibrium, solve for the F needed, and check whether F ≤ μ_s N. If not, the body slides and F = μ_k N.
4. For problems with several contacts, consider each possible mode of slipping (or tipping) and find which happens first.

Worked example (incline): a 50 kg block rests on a 20° incline with μ_s = 0.3.
- tan 20° = 0.364 > 0.3, so friction alone cannot hold it: it slides down.
- Force P parallel to the slope needed to push it up at constant speed (taking μ = 0.3): P = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ) = 490.5 × (0.342 + 0.282) ≈ 306 N.
- The minimum parallel force just to stop it sliding down: P = mg(sin θ − μ cos θ) ≈ 29.5 N, because friction now acts up the slope.

Worked example (ladder): a uniform ladder leans against a smooth wall with its foot on a rough floor (μ_s = 0.4). Taking moments about the foot, the wall reaction is N_w = W/(2 tan θ), where θ is the ladder's angle to the floor; this must be provided by floor friction, so W/(2 tan θ) ≤ μW, giving tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ) = 1.25. The ladder is safe only if θ ≥ 51.3°.

Belt friction (flat belt or rope round a drum): T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ), where T₂ is the larger (tight-side) tension, T₁ the smaller and β the angle of wrap in radians. With μ = 0.3 and β = π (half a turn), T₂/T₁ = e^(0.3π) ≈ 2.57, so holding a 500 N load needs only about 195 N. This is why a rope wrapped several times around a bollard can hold a ship.

Wedges and screws: applications where friction is used to hold or lift loads; self-locking happens when friction prevents back-driving.

Exam tips: always draw friction opposing the tendency to move, state whether slip is impending, and check your assumption at the end.

notes.h: Analysis of structures: trusses and frames
notes.body:
Engineering structures are analysed by breaking them into parts and applying equilibrium to each part. Two classes of structure are treated differently.

Trusses: straight members joined at their ends by pins, with loads only at the joints. Every member is a two-force member carrying pure tension or compression.

Method of joints:
- Find support reactions using the whole truss as a free body.
- At each joint, ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 (two equations), so start at a joint with at most two unknowns.
- Assume every unknown member force is tension (arrow pulling away from the joint); a negative answer means compression.

Worked example: a triangular truss has span 6 m (supports A and B) and apex C 4 m above mid-span, so each sloping member is 5 m long (3–4–5 triangle). A 12 kN load acts down at C.
- Reactions: 6 kN up at each support.
- Joint A, vertical: 6 + F_AC × (4/5) = 0, so F_AC = −7.5 kN (7.5 kN compression).
- Joint A, horizontal: F_AB + F_AC × (3/5) = 0, so F_AB = +4.5 kN (4.5 kN tension).

Method of sections: cut the truss through three members (not all meeting at one point) and take moments about the intersection of two of them to find the third directly. This is fastest when only a few member forces are needed.

Zero-force members:
- If two non-collinear members meet at an unloaded joint, both carry zero force.
- If three members meet at an unloaded joint and two are collinear, the third carries zero force.
Spotting these first saves time.

Simple truss: built up from a basic triangle by adding two members and one joint at a time; such a truss satisfies m = 2j − 3 and is rigid and statically determinate when properly supported.

Frames and machines: structures containing at least one multi-force member (a member with forces at more than two points, or loaded along its length). These members carry bending as well as axial force, so you cannot treat them as simple links.
- Dismember the structure: draw an FBD of each member.
- Forces at a connecting pin are equal and opposite on the two members (Newton's third law).
- Identify any two-force members first: their force direction is known (along the line joining their pins), which reduces the unknowns.
- Machines (pliers, cutters, linkages) transmit and change forces; the same method gives the mechanical advantage, the ratio of output force to input force.

The learning outcomes include analysing a bridge-like structure and experimental results. In a lab truss, measured member strains (and so forces, using F = EAε) can be compared with the pin-jointed predictions; differences come from joint rigidity, self-weight, load eccentricity and measurement error.

Exam tips: state the sign convention, check one equation at the end (for example at the last joint), and in frames always identify two-force members before writing equations.

notes.h: Distributed forces and centre of gravity
notes.body:
Many forces are spread over a length, area or volume rather than acting at a point: self-weight, wind pressure, water pressure, soil pressure, floor loads. For equilibrium of a rigid body, a distributed force can be replaced by a single resultant acting at the right place.

Centre of gravity and centroid:
- The centre of gravity G is the point through which the resultant of a body's weight acts.
- For a body of uniform density, G coincides with the centroid of its volume; for a thin uniform plate, with the centroid of its area.
- Centroid of an area: x̄ = ∫x dA/∫dA and ȳ = ∫y dA/∫dA.
- Any axis of symmetry contains the centroid.

Standard centroids:
- Rectangle: at its centre.
- Triangle: one third of the height from its base (two thirds from the apex).
- Semicircle of radius r: 4r/(3π) from the diameter.

Composite bodies: split into simple parts with known centroids, then
x̄ = ΣA_i x_i/ΣA_i and ȳ = ΣA_i y_i/ΣA_i.
Holes are treated as negative areas.

Worked example: an L-shaped plate made from a 100 × 20 mm horizontal strip (from x = 0 to 100 mm, y = 0 to 20 mm) and a 20 × 80 mm vertical strip standing on its left end (x = 0 to 20 mm, y = 20 to 100 mm).
- Part 1: A = 2000 mm², centroid (50, 10).
- Part 2: A = 1600 mm², centroid (10, 60).
- x̄ = (2000 × 50 + 1600 × 10)/3600 = 32.2 mm; ȳ = (2000 × 10 + 1600 × 60)/3600 = 32.2 mm.
- The two values are equal because the shape is symmetric about the line y = x (an equal-leg angle). Note the centroid lies outside the material, in the corner.

Distributed loads on beams: a line load w(x) (N/m) has a resultant equal to the area under the load diagram, acting through the centroid of that area.
- Uniform load w over length L: resultant wL at mid-length.
- Triangular load rising from 0 to w₀ over length L: resultant w₀L/2 acting L/3 from the larger end (2L/3 from the zero end).
- Trapezoidal loads: split into a rectangle and a triangle.

Worked example: a simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a load that increases linearly from 0 at A to 12 kN/m at B.
- Resultant = ½ × 12 × 6 = 36 kN, acting 4 m from A.
- Moments about A: R_B × 6 = 36 × 4, so R_B = 24 kN; R_A = 12 kN.

Fluid pressure on a submerged surface is a distributed load of this kind (it increases linearly with depth), which is why the resultant acts at two-thirds depth on a vertical wall whose top is at the surface.

Theorems of Pappus–Guldinus: the surface area (or volume) of a body of revolution equals the length of the generating curve (or the generating area) times the distance travelled by its centroid.

Important: the single-resultant replacement is valid for finding reactions and overall equilibrium, but not for finding internal forces, which depend on how the load is actually distributed.

Exam tips: tabulate A, x, Ax, y, Ay for composite shapes, and sketch the resultant on the load diagram before taking moments.

notes.h: Internal forces and moments in structures
notes.body:
External loads on a member are carried through it by internal forces. To find them, cut the member at a section and apply equilibrium to the part on either side.

Internal force components at a section of a 2D member:
- Normal (axial) force N, along the member's axis; tension positive.
- Shear force V, perpendicular to the axis.
- Bending moment M.
The forces and moment on the two faces of the cut are equal and opposite (Newton's third law), so you may analyse whichever side is simpler.

Sign convention (state yours): shear force positive when the resultant of the forces to the left of the section acts upwards; bending moment positive when sagging (beam concave upwards, bottom fibres in tension).

Method of sections for beams:
1. Find support reactions.
2. Cut at distance x from one end; draw the FBD of one part with N, V and M at the cut in their positive directions.
3. Apply ΣF and ΣM = 0 to find N, V and M as functions of x.

Worked example: a 5 m simply supported beam carries a 20 kN point load 2 m from the left support A.
- Reactions: R_A = 20 × 3/5 = 12 kN, R_B = 8 kN.
- For 0 < x < 2 m: V = 12 kN and M = 12x (sagging), reaching 24 kN·m under the load.
- For 2 < x < 5 m: V = 12 − 20 = −8 kN, and M = 12x − 20(x − 2), which falls from 24 kN·m to zero at B.

Relationships between load, shear and moment (with w the downward load per unit length):
- dV/dx = −w
- dM/dx = V
So the bending moment is maximum where the shear force is zero or changes sign; a point load causes a jump in V; on an unloaded length V is constant and M varies linearly; under a uniform load V is linear and M is parabolic.

Standard results:
- Cantilever of length L with uniform load w: maximum (hogging) moment wL²/2 at the fixed end. For L = 3 m and w = 4 kN/m, M = 18 kN·m.
- Simply supported span with uniform load w: maximum moment wL²/8 at mid-span.
- Simply supported span with central point load P: maximum moment PL/4.

Shear force and bending moment diagrams plot V and M along the member. Draw them under the loading diagram with key values (supports, load points, maxima, zero crossings) marked.

Why it matters: internal forces lead to stresses (σ = N/A for axial load, σ = My/I for bending), which are compared with material strength. You will develop this in later solid mechanics modules.

Members of frames: the same procedure applies to each member after dismembering the frame; at a corner, the internal forces of one member become components of the next.

Exam tips: always show the FBD of the cut part with assumed positive directions, write V(x) and M(x) for each region between load changes, and use dM/dx = V to check your diagrams.

cards.b: A fixed quantity of matter: energy may cross the boundary as heat or work, but mass cannot.
A region in space through which mass flows, such as a pump, turbine or nozzle.
Intensive properties (p, T, ρ) do not depend on the amount of matter; extensive ones (V, m, U) do.
If two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
R ≈ 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), from R = R̄/M with R̄ = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K) and M ≈ 28.97 kg/kmol.
A substance that deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small.
Fluid in contact with a solid surface moves with the same velocity as the surface.
Pressure measured relative to local atmospheric pressure: p_gauge = p_abs − p_atm.
p = p₀ + ρgh for a fluid of constant density at rest, h measured downwards from where p = p₀.
h = p/(ρg): the height of a column of fluid that would produce pressure p.

cards.f: Resultant force on a submerged plane surface
cards.b: F = ρ g h_c A, where h_c is the depth of the centroid of the area.
h_cp = h_c + I_G/(h_c A); it lies below the centroid.
The buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced, ρ_fluid g V_displaced.
ṁ = ρAV, with V the mean velocity normal to the area A.
A₁V₁ = A₂V₂: halving the diameter quarters the area and multiplies the velocity by 4.
p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant: steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline, with no work or heat transfer.
Speed of a free jet from a tank with head h, ignoring losses: V = √(2gh).
Re = ρVD/μ, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces; pipe flow is usually laminar below about 2000–2300.
A model and full-size flow behave alike when geometric similarity holds and the relevant dimensionless groups (e.g. Re) match.

cards.f: First Law for a closed system
cards.b: Q − W = ΔU (+ΔKE + ΔPE), with heat into and work out of the system positive.
No. Heat and work are path functions; internal energy is a property (state function).

cards.f: Boundary work for a quasi-static process
cards.b: W = ∫p dV, the area under the process curve on a p–V diagram.

cards.f: Isothermal work for an ideal gas
cards.b: W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = mRT ln(p₁/p₂).
W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1) for pVⁿ = constant.

cards.f: c_p − c_v for an ideal gas
cards.b: Equals R, the specific gas constant; γ = c_p/c_v ≈ 1.4 for air.
h = u + pv: internal energy plus flow work, the natural energy property for flowing fluids.
Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h₂ − h₁) + (V₂² − V₁²)/2 + g(z₂ − z₁)].
Adiabatic, no work, negligible ΔKE, so h₂ = h₁; for an ideal gas the temperature is unchanged.

cards.f: Ideal pump power for a liquid
cards.b: Ẇ = QΔp (or ṁvΔp), e.g. 0.01 m³/s through 500 kPa needs 5 kW.
V₂ = √(V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂)), with h in J/kg.

cards.f: Sign of compressor work in the SFEE
cards.b: Negative (work out of the CV positive), showing that power must be supplied.

cards.f: Moment of a force about a point
cards.b: M = F × d, with d the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action; vector form M = r × F.
The moment of a force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components about that point.
Two equal, opposite, parallel non-collinear forces; zero resultant force and the same moment Fd about every point.
A force can be moved to any point provided a couple equal to its moment about that point is added.
M_z = x F_y − y F_x (anticlockwise positive).

cards.f: Resultant of 3 kN east and 4 kN north
cards.b: 5 kN at about 53.1° north of east.
ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 about any point.
Two force components and a moment.
A member loaded at two points only: the forces are equal, opposite and along the line joining those points.
The three forces must be concurrent or parallel for equilibrium.
Three independent reactions that are neither all parallel nor all concurrent.

cards.f: Why take moments about a pin?
cards.b: The pin's two unknown reaction components pass through it and drop out of the moment equation.
F ≤ μ_s N; at impending motion F = μ_s N.
φ with tan φ = μ_s; a block on an incline is about to slide when the incline angle equals φ.
F = μ_k N during sliding, with μ_k usually a little smaller than μ_s.
T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ), with T₂ the tight-side tension and β the wrap angle in radians.
On each body, opposing that body's relative motion or tendency to move.

cards.f: Minimum ladder angle (smooth wall, rough floor)
cards.b: tan θ ≥ 1/(2μ) for a uniform ladder, with θ measured from the floor.
Straight members, frictionless pins, loads only at joints, so members carry axial force only.
m = 2j − 3 for a simple truss built from a triangle by adding two members and one joint at a time.
Two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint: both zero. Three members with two collinear at an unloaded joint: the third is zero.
Cut through up to three members and take moments about the intersection of two to find the third directly.
A frame has at least one multi-force member carrying bending; a truss has only two-force members.
Ratio of output force to input force of a machine.
x̄ = ΣA_i x_i/ΣA_i (holes as negative areas).
One third of the height from the base.
4r/(3π) from the diameter.

cards.f: Resultant of a triangular load 0 to w₀ over L
cards.b: w₀L/2 acting L/3 from the larger end.
They coincide for a body of uniform density in a uniform gravitational field.
Area (volume) of revolution = length of generating curve (generating area) × distance travelled by its centroid.

cards.f: Internal force components in a 2D member
cards.b: Axial (normal) force N, shear force V and bending moment M.
Equals the shear force V, so M is maximum where V = 0 or changes sign.
Equals −w, minus the distributed load intensity.

cards.f: Maximum moment in a cantilever with UDL
cards.b: wL²/2 (hogging) at the fixed end.
Bends a beam concave upwards, with the bottom fibres in tension; usually taken as positive.

cards.f: Effect of a point load on the SFD
cards.b: A sudden jump equal to the load; the BMD has a change of slope there.

questions.q: What is the density of air at 100 kPa and 27 °C, treating it as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)?
questions.why: ρ = p/(RT) = 100 000/(287 × 300) ≈ 1.16 kg/m³. 12.9 kg/m³ uses the Celsius temperature (27) instead of kelvin. 0.00116 kg/m³ puts p in kPa (100) but R in J/(kg·K) (287), a factor of 1000 mismatch. 0.861 kg/m³ is the specific volume RT/p in m³/kg, the reciprocal of density.

questions.q: Which of the following is an intensive property?
questions.why: Temperature does not depend on how much matter is present, so it is intensive. Volume, mass and total internal energy all double if the system is doubled, so they are extensive (dividing them by mass gives specific, intensive versions).

questions.q: Distinguish between a closed system and a control volume, giving an engineering example of each, and explain why the choice matters when applying the First Law.
markScheme: Closed system: fixed mass; heat and work cross boundary, mass does not; e.g. gas in sealed piston–cylinder
Control volume: fixed region; mass flows across; e.g. turbine, pump, nozzle
Closed: Q − W = ΔU; open: must account for energy carried by mass flow (enthalpy, KE, PE) – SFEE
Choice determines what crosses the boundary and which equation and terms apply
questions.modelAnswer: A closed system (control mass) contains a fixed quantity of matter; its boundary may move, and heat and work may cross it, but no mass does, for example gas trapped in a sealed piston–cylinder. A control volume is a region in space with mass flowing in and out, for example a turbine, pump or nozzle. The choice matters because it determines what crosses the boundary. For a closed system the First Law is Q − W = ΔU (+ΔKE + ΔPE). For a control volume the energy carried in and out with the flowing mass must also be included, together with the flow work needed to push it across the boundary. This leads to enthalpy and the steady-flow energy equation, Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz].

questions.q: What is the absolute pressure at a depth of 10 m in fresh water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², atmospheric pressure 101.3 kPa)?
questions.why: Gauge pressure = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98.1 kPa; absolute = 98.1 + 101.3 ≈ 199.4 kPa. 98.1 kPa is the gauge pressure only, missing the atmosphere acting on the free surface. 3.2 kPa subtracts the hydrostatic pressure from atmospheric (101.3 − 98.1) instead of adding it. 111.1 kPa adds only ρg = 9.81 kPa, i.e. forgets to multiply by the depth.

questions.q: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge at the water surface. At what depth does the resultant hydrostatic force act?
questions.why: h_cp = h_c + I_G/(h_c A) = 1.5 + (2 × 3³/12)/(1.5 × 6) = 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 m, two-thirds of the depth, because the pressure distribution is triangular. 1.5 m is the centroid, where the average pressure acts but not the resultant. 1.0 m is one-third of the depth, measured from the wrong end of the triangle. 3.0 m is the bottom edge, where the pressure is greatest but the resultant does not act.

questions.q: A U-tube manometer containing mercury (relative density 13.6) is connected across an orifice plate in a horizontal water pipe. The mercury levels differ by 200 mm. Find the pressure difference across the orifice. Explain why the answer differs from the case where the pipe carries air.
markScheme: Equal pressures at the same level in the continuous mercury
Water above both mercury surfaces: Δp = (ρ_Hg − ρ_w) g Δh
With air, the gas column weight is negligible: Δp = ρ_Hg g Δh ≈ 26.7 kPa
Explains the difference: the water column on the low side partly balances the mercury
questions.modelAnswer: Take the level of the lower mercury surface. The pressure is the same at this level in both limbs because the mercury is continuous. On the high-pressure side: p₁ + ρ_w g(y + Δh). On the low-pressure side: p₂ + ρ_w g y + ρ_Hg g Δh, where y is the distance from the pipe centre down to the upper mercury surface. Equating gives p₁ − p₂ = (ρ_Hg − ρ_w) g Δh = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.2 ≈ 24.7 kPa. If the pipe carried air, the weight of the air columns would be negligible, giving Δp = ρ_Hg g Δh = 13 600 × 9.81 × 0.2 ≈ 26.7 kPa. With water, the column of water standing above the depressed mercury surface partly balances the mercury, so the same reading means a smaller pressure difference.

questions.q: Water flows at 2 m/s in a horizontal 100 mm pipe that contracts to 50 mm. Neglecting losses, what is the pressure drop from the large to the small section?
questions.why: Continuity: V₂ = 2 × (100/50)² = 8 m/s. Bernoulli: Δp = ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) = ½ × 1000 × (64 − 4) = 30 kPa. 6 kPa uses V₂ = 4 m/s, scaling velocity with the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio (½ × 1000 × (16 − 4)). 32 kPa forgets to subtract the upstream kinetic energy (½ × 1000 × 64). 2 kPa is ½ρV₁², the upstream dynamic pressure only.

questions.q: Which condition is NOT required for Bernoulli's equation p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant to apply?
questions.why: Bernoulli requires steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline (with no work or heat transfer). Laminar flow is not a condition: a laminar flow can still have large viscous losses, and the equation is routinely applied to turbulent mean flows outside boundary layers where friction is small. Steady flow, incompressibility and negligible viscosity are genuine conditions.

questions.q: Water drains from a large open tank through a small hole 5 m below the free surface. (a) Estimate the jet speed, stating the assumptions. (b) If the hole has area 1 × 10⁻³ m² and the tank has plan area 2 m², estimate the initial rate at which the water level falls.
markScheme: Bernoulli from free surface (p = p_atm, V ≈ 0, z = 5 m) to jet (p = p_atm, z = 0)
Assumptions: steady (quasi-steady), incompressible, inviscid, along a streamline; large tank so surface velocity ≈ 0
Level falls at Q/A_tank ≈ 4.95 × 10⁻³ m/s (about 5 mm/s); real value lower due to jet contraction/losses
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Apply Bernoulli along a streamline from the free surface (1) to the jet just outside the hole (2). Both are at atmospheric pressure. The surface velocity is negligible because the tank is large, and z₁ − z₂ = 5 m. Then V₂ = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) ≈ 9.9 m/s. Assumptions: quasi-steady flow (the level falls slowly), incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline, and uniform jet velocity. (b) Volume flow Q = AV = 1 × 10⁻³ × 9.9 = 9.9 × 10⁻³ m³/s. A mass balance on the tank gives A_tank dh/dt = −Q, so the level falls at 9.9 × 10⁻³/2 ≈ 4.95 × 10⁻³ m/s, about 5 mm/s. In practice the jet contracts (vena contracta) and there are small losses, so the real flow is lower; a discharge coefficient is used to correct for this.

questions.q: 0.5 kg of air (c_v = 0.718, c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K)) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 400 K. How much heat is supplied?
questions.why: At constant pressure Q = mc_pΔT = 0.5 × 1.005 × 100 = 50.25 kJ (= ΔU of 35.9 kJ plus boundary work of 14.35 kJ). 35.9 kJ uses c_v, which gives the heat only for a constant-volume process. 14.35 kJ is the boundary work mRΔT, not the heat. 86.15 kJ adds the c_p and c_v results together, double-counting the internal energy change.

questions.q: Which statement about heat and work is correct?
options: Both are properties of the system
Both depend on the process path, not just the end states
Heat depends on the path but work does not
Their sum is always zero in any process
questions.why: Heat and work are energy transfers that depend on the path: the same end states can be reached with different amounts of heat and work. They are not properties, which only depend on the state, so the claim that both are properties is wrong. Work is path-dependent too (it is the area under the p–V curve, which differs between paths). Their difference, not their sum, equals ΔU (Q − W = ΔU), so Q − W is zero only when ΔU = 0, for example over a complete cycle or in the isothermal expansion of an ideal gas; their sum has no general rule.

questions.q: 0.5 kg of air at 300 K expands isothermally and quasi-statically to twice its original volume. Calculate the work done, the change in internal energy and the heat transfer, stating your sign convention. Explain the result physically.
markScheme: Sign convention stated (Q in, W out positive; Q − W = ΔU)
W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 0.5 × 0.287 × 300 × ln 2 ≈ 29.8 kJ (done by the gas)
Ideal gas: U depends only on T, so ΔU = 0
Q = W ≈ 29.8 kJ supplied
Physical explanation: heat added exactly balances work output to keep T constant
questions.modelAnswer: Convention: heat supplied to the system and work done by the system are positive, so Q − W = ΔU. For an isothermal quasi-static process of an ideal gas, W = ∫p dV = mRT ln(V₂/V₁) = 0.5 × 0.287 × 300 × ln 2 ≈ 29.8 kJ, positive, so the gas does work on its surroundings. For an ideal gas internal energy depends only on temperature, so with T constant ΔU = 0. The First Law then gives Q = W ≈ 29.8 kJ: this much heat must be supplied. Physically, as the gas expands it pushes the piston and does work; to keep its temperature constant, an equal amount of energy must flow in as heat. Without it the gas would cool, as in an adiabatic expansion.

questions.q: Air (c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K)) flows at 0.5 kg/s through an adiabatic compressor, entering at 300 K and leaving at 450 K. Neglecting changes in KE and PE, what power is required?
questions.why: Ẇ = ṁc_p(T₁ − T₂) = 0.5 × 1.005 × (−150) = −75.4 kW, so 75.4 kW must be supplied. 53.9 kW uses c_v (0.718) instead of c_p, ignoring flow work. 150.8 kW forgets to multiply by the mass flow rate of 0.5 kg/s. 21.5 kW uses R (0.287) instead of c_p.

questions.q: Steam passes through a throttling valve that is adiabatic, does no work, and has negligible change in kinetic energy. Which quantity stays the same across the valve?
questions.why: The SFEE with Q̇ = 0, Ẇ = 0 and negligible ΔKE and ΔPE gives h₂ = h₁, so enthalpy is constant. Pressure falls, which is the purpose of the valve. Temperature stays constant only for an ideal gas; for steam it generally changes. Entropy increases, because throttling is an irreversible process.

questions.q: Air enters an adiabatic nozzle at 500 K with a velocity of 10 m/s and leaves at 450 K. Treating air as an ideal gas with c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), find the exit velocity. State the assumptions and explain one common unit error.
markScheme: SFEE with Q̇ = 0, Ẇ = 0, Δz ≈ 0: h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2
Assumptions: steady flow, adiabatic, ideal gas with constant c_p, negligible PE change
Unit error: using c_p in kJ/(kg·K) with V² in m²/s², which gives a velocity far too small (about 14 m/s)
questions.modelAnswer: For steady flow through an adiabatic nozzle with no work and negligible change in height, the SFEE reduces to h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2. For an ideal gas with constant c_p, h₁ − h₂ = c_p(T₁ − T₂) = 1005 × 50 = 50 250 J/kg. Then V₂ = √(V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂)) = √(100 + 100 500) ≈ 317 m/s. Assumptions: steady flow, adiabatic walls, no shaft work, constant c_p and negligible potential energy change. A common error is to use c_p = 1.005 (kJ/(kg·K)) with velocities in m/s: this gives √(100 + 2 × 1.005 × 50) ≈ 14.2 m/s, far too small, because kinetic energy per unit mass in m²/s² is in J/kg, not kJ/kg.

questions.q: A 500 N force is applied at the end of a 0.4 m spanner, acting at 30° to the spanner's length. What moment does it exert about the bolt?
questions.why: Only the component perpendicular to the spanner, 500 sin 30° = 250 N, has a lever arm: M = 250 × 0.4 = 100 N·m. 200 N·m uses the full force (500 × 0.4), ignoring the angle. 173 N·m uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°, taking the component along the spanner, which passes through the bolt. 250 N·m is the perpendicular component (250 N) quoted without multiplying by the lever arm.

questions.q: Which statement about a couple is correct?
options: It has a resultant force equal to the sum of the two forces
Its moment is the same about every point
Its moment depends on the point about which it is taken
It can be balanced by a single force
questions.why: A couple has zero resultant force and its moment Fd is the same about every point, so it is a free vector. Adding the two forces gives zero, not a non-zero resultant. Its moment does not depend on the reference point. A single force always has a non-zero resultant, so it cannot balance a couple; only an equal and opposite couple can.

questions.q: Forces of 3 kN acting due east and 4 kN acting due north are applied at the origin, and a 2 kN force acts due south at the point (3 m, 0). Find the resultant force and its moment about the origin, and hence where the resultant's line of action crosses the x-axis.
markScheme: Components: R_x = 3 kN, R_y = 4 − 2 = 2 kN; R = √13 ≈ 3.61 kN at 33.7° above east
Moment about O: only the 2 kN force has a lever arm: M = x F_y = 3 × (−2) = −6 kN·m (clockwise)
Resultant's line crosses x-axis at x where x R_y = M: x = −6/2 = −3 m
Correct signs/convention stated
questions.modelAnswer: Resolve: R_x = 3 kN and R_y = 4 − 2 = 2 kN, so R = √(3² + 2²) = √13 ≈ 3.61 kN at tan⁻¹(2/3) ≈ 33.7° above east. Moments about the origin (anticlockwise positive): the 3 kN and 4 kN forces pass through O and contribute nothing; the 2 kN force at (3, 0) acting in −y gives M = x F_y = 3 × (−2) = −6 kN·m, i.e. 6 kN·m clockwise. The single resultant must have the same moment about O. If it crosses the x-axis at (x, 0), its moment is x R_y = 2x, so 2x = −6 and x = −3 m. The resultant line of action passes through (−3 m, 0).

questions.q: A horizontal beam AB, 4 m long and of negligible weight, is pinned at A and held at B by a cable to the wall above A, making 30° with the beam. A 10 kN load hangs at B. What is the cable tension?
questions.why: Moments about A: T sin 30° × 4 = 10 × 4, so T = 20 kN. 10 kN assumes the cable simply carries the load directly, ignoring its angle. 11.5 kN uses cos 30° in place of sin 30° (10/0.866). 17.3 kN is the horizontal pin reaction T cos 30°, not the tension.

questions.q: Which support provides two reaction force components and a reaction moment in a 2D problem?
questions.why: A fixed (built-in) support prevents translation in both directions and rotation, so it provides two forces and a moment. A roller provides only one force, normal to its surface. A pin provides two force components but no moment. A cable provides one tensile force along its length.

questions.q: For the beam of the previous question (4 m long, pinned at A, cable at B at 30° to the beam, 10 kN at B), the beam's own weight of 2 kN acts at mid-length. Draw the free body diagram and find the cable tension and the pin reactions at A.
markScheme: FBD: A_x, A_y at pin; T along cable at 30°; 10 kN at B; 2 kN at 2 m
Moments about A: T sin 30° × 4 = 10 × 4 + 2 × 2 → T = 22 kN
ΣFx: A_x = T cos 30° ≈ 19.1 kN (wall pushes outward)
ΣFy: A_y = 12 − 22 × 0.5 = 1 kN upwards
Check, e.g. moments about B or about the cable's wall anchor
questions.modelAnswer: Free body diagram: pin reactions A_x and A_y at A; cable tension T at B acting along the cable towards the wall anchor, at 30° above the beam; 2 kN down at 2 m; 10 kN down at 4 m. Moments about A: T sin 30° × 4 − 10 × 4 − 2 × 2 = 0, so 2T = 44 and T = 22 kN. Horizontal: the cable's horizontal component, T cos 30° = 19.1 kN, pulls the beam towards the wall, so the pin pushes outwards with A_x = 19.1 kN. Vertical: A_y + T sin 30° − 12 = 0, so A_y = 12 − 11 = 1 kN upwards. Check by moments about B: A_y × 4 − 2 × 2 = 4 − 4 = 0, as required (T and the 10 kN load pass through B).

questions.q: A block rests on a 20° incline with μ_s = 0.3. What happens if it is released from rest?
options: It stays at rest because 0.3 > sin 20°
It slides only if its mass exceeds a critical value
It slides, because tan 20° ≈ 0.36 exceeds μ_s
It stays at rest because μ_s > 0
questions.why: Sliding starts when the incline angle exceeds the angle of friction, i.e. when tan θ > μ_s: tan 20° = 0.364 > 0.3, so it slides. Any non-zero μ_s is not enough on its own; it must be large enough. Comparing μ_s with sin 20° (0.342) is the wrong test: the condition comes from F/N = tan θ, not sin θ (and 0.3 is not greater than 0.342 anyway). Mass cancels from both the driving force and the friction limit, so it does not matter.

questions.q: A rope is wrapped half a turn (β = π) round a fixed post with μ = 0.3. The tight side holds a 500 N load. What is the least force on the slack side that stops it slipping?
questions.why: T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ) = e^(0.3π) ≈ 2.57, so T₁ = 500/2.57 ≈ 195 N. 350 N treats the post like a flat surface, subtracting a Coulomb friction force μ × 500 = 150 N from the load. 312 N uses a quarter turn (β = π/2) instead of a half turn: 500/e^(0.3π/2) ≈ 312 N. 1283 N multiplies by e^(μβ) instead of dividing, which is the tension needed to haul the load upwards rather than to hold it.

questions.q: A uniform ladder of weight W leans against a smooth vertical wall with its foot on a rough floor (μ_s = 0.4). Find the smallest angle between the ladder and the floor for which it can stand without slipping.
markScheme: FBD: W at mid-length; floor normal N_f and friction F; wall normal N_w (smooth: no friction)
ΣFy: N_f = W; ΣFx: F = N_w
Moments about foot: N_w L sin θ = W (L/2) cos θ → N_w = W/(2 tan θ)
No slip: F ≤ μN_f → W/(2 tan θ) ≤ 0.4W → tan θ ≥ 1.25
questions.modelAnswer: Let θ be the angle between the ladder and the floor and L its length. Forces: weight W at mid-length; at the floor, normal reaction N_f and friction F towards the wall; at the smooth wall, a horizontal normal reaction N_w only. Vertical equilibrium gives N_f = W and horizontal equilibrium gives F = N_w. Moments about the foot: N_w × L sin θ = W × (L/2) cos θ, so N_w = W/(2 tan θ). The ladder does not slip if F ≤ μ_s N_f, i.e. W/(2 tan θ) ≤ 0.4W, so tan θ ≥ 1/(2 × 0.4) = 1.25 and θ ≥ 51.3°. Steeper ladders are safer because they need less friction at the foot.

questions.q: A triangular truss spans 6 m with its apex 4 m above mid-span; 12 kN acts downwards at the apex. What is the force in each sloping member?
questions.why: Each reaction is 6 kN. At a support, the sloping member's vertical component must balance it: F × (4/5) = 6, so F = 7.5 kN, compression. 6 kN is the reaction itself. 4.5 kN tension is the force in the horizontal tie. 10 kN comes from dividing by 3/5 instead of 4/5, i.e. using the horizontal instead of the vertical component.

questions.q: At an unloaded truss joint, only two members meet and they are not collinear. What are their forces?
options: Equal to half the nearest support reaction
Impossible to say without the method of sections
questions.why: Each member's force has a component perpendicular to the other member, which nothing else can balance, so both must be zero. 'Equal and opposite, non-zero' would only be possible if the members were collinear. The support reaction has no direct bearing on an unloaded internal joint. The method of sections is not needed: joint equilibrium settles it immediately.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a truss and a frame, and outline how you would find the forces in the members of a simple A-frame in which one leg is a multi-force member. Why can a frame not be analysed entirely by the method of joints?
markScheme: Truss: only two-force members, pin joints, loads at joints → axial force only
Frame: at least one multi-force member (loads at >2 points or along length) → bending as well as axial force
Procedure: reactions from whole structure; dismember; FBD each member; equal and opposite pin forces; identify two-force members first
Method of joints assumes member forces act along members; not true for multi-force members whose pin forces have unknown direction
Correct mention of number of equations (3 per member) vs unknowns
questions.modelAnswer: In a truss every member is a two-force member: pin-ended, straight and loaded only at its ends, so it carries only axial tension or compression, and joint equilibrium (two equations per joint) gives the member forces. A frame contains at least one multi-force member, loaded at more than two points or along its length, which carries shear and bending as well as axial force. For an A-frame, first find the support reactions from the whole structure. Then dismember it, drawing an FBD of each member, with the pin forces between members equal and opposite on each. Any two-force member (such as the cross-bar if it is loaded only at its pins) has a force along its own line, which removes an unknown. Each multi-force member then gives three equilibrium equations. The method of joints cannot be used on its own because it assumes each member's force acts along its axis; for a multi-force member the pin force can act in any direction, so both of its components are unknown.

questions.q: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a load that rises linearly from 0 at A to 12 kN/m at B. What is the reaction at B?
questions.why: Resultant = ½ × 12 × 6 = 36 kN acting 4 m from A (two-thirds of the way towards the larger end). Moments about A: R_B × 6 = 36 × 4, so R_B = 24 kN. 12 kN is the reaction at A. 18 kN places the resultant at mid-span, as for a uniform load. 36 kN is the total load, not a reaction.

questions.q: An L-shaped plate is made from a 100 × 20 mm strip lying along the x-axis (0 ≤ x ≤ 100, 0 ≤ y ≤ 20) and a 20 × 80 mm strip standing on its left end (0 ≤ x ≤ 20, 20 ≤ y ≤ 100). What is x̄?
questions.why: x̄ = (2000 × 50 + 1600 × 10)/3600 = 116 000/3600 = 32.2 mm. 30.0 mm averages the two part centroids (50 and 10) without weighting by area. 50.0 mm is the centroid of the horizontal strip alone. 27.8 mm swaps the areas, weighting x = 50 by 1600 and x = 10 by 2000 ((1600 × 50 + 2000 × 10)/3600).

questions.q: Explain why a distributed load may be replaced by a single resultant force when finding support reactions, but not when finding the bending moment at a section within the loaded length. Illustrate with a uniformly loaded simply supported beam.
markScheme: Resultant = area under load diagram, acting at its centroid; gives same total force and moment about any point → same reactions
Internal forces depend on load on one side of the cut only
Example: UDL w on span L, reactions wL/2 either way
With a point load wL at mid-span, M_max = wL²/4 instead of the correct wL²/8 (twice too large)
questions.modelAnswer: A distributed load and its resultant (equal to the area under the load diagram, acting through its centroid) produce the same total force and the same moment about any point. Overall equilibrium, and therefore the support reactions, is unchanged. Internal forces at a section, however, depend only on the load acting on one side of the cut, and the way it is spread along that part matters. For a simply supported beam of span L with a uniform load w, the reactions are wL/2 whether the load is distributed or replaced by wL at mid-span. But the true mid-span moment is wL²/8, whereas the point-load replacement gives (wL)L/4 = wL²/4, twice too large. To find M at a section, cut first, then replace only the load on the free body by its resultant.

questions.q: A 5 m simply supported beam carries 20 kN at 2 m from the left support A. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.why: R_A = 20 × 3/5 = 12 kN, and M under the load = 12 × 2 = 24 kN·m (= Pab/L = 20 × 2 × 3/5). 25 kN·m uses PL/4, which applies only to a central load. 40 kN·m is P × a (20 × 2), ignoring the reaction. 20 kN·m is the load value in kN mistaken for a moment.

questions.q: At a point on a beam where the shear force changes sign from positive to negative, the bending moment is:
questions.why: Since dM/dx = V, M increases while V is positive and decreases once V is negative, so M has a local maximum there. Zero moment occurs at points of contraflexure or pinned ends, not where V changes sign. A local minimum would need V to go from negative to positive. M jumps only where a concentrated moment (couple) is applied, not at a change of sign of V.

questions.q: A cantilever of length 3 m is fixed at A and free at B. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 4 kN/m along its whole length. Using the method of sections, derive expressions for the shear force and bending moment at distance x from the free end, and sketch the diagrams with key values.
markScheme: Cut at x from B; FBD of free-end part carries load 4x acting at x/2
Shear force magnitude V = 4x kN (sign stated by convention, e.g. positive with upward resultant on the left part)
M = −4x²/2 = −2x² kN·m (hogging)
At the fixed end x = 3 m: |V| = 12 kN, M = −18 kN·m
Sketch: linear SFD from 0 to 12 kN; parabolic BMD from 0 to −18 kN·m
questions.modelAnswer: Cut the beam at distance x from the free end B and consider the free-end part. It carries a load of 4x kN acting at x/2 from the cut. For equilibrium, the internal shear force at the cut must balance it: V = 4x kN in magnitude. With the beam drawn fixed at the left and free at the right, the part to the right of the cut is pulled down by the load, so on the usual convention (shear positive when the resultant to the left of the section acts upwards) V = +4x. The moment at the cut is M = −4x × x/2 = −2x² kN·m: hogging, tension on top. At the fixed end (x = 3 m), the shear is 12 kN and the moment is −18 kN·m (= wL²/2). The SFD is a straight line from 0 at B to 12 kN at A; the BMD is a parabola from 0 at B to −18 kN·m at A, steepest at the support, consistent with dM/dx = V.

questions.q:
A small air compressor and aftercooler system operates steadily. Air (ideal gas, c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K)) enters the compressor at 100 kPa and 300 K with a mass flow rate of 0.5 kg/s and leaves at 450 K. The compressor is adiabatic. The air then passes through an aftercooler (no work) in which it is cooled back to 310 K at constant pressure, transferring heat to cooling water that enters at 15 °C and leaves at 25 °C (c_water = 4.18 kJ/(kg·K)). Kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible.
(a) Sketch the system, showing the control volumes and everything that crosses their boundaries. [3]
(b) State the steady-flow energy equation and the assumptions needed to simplify it for each device. [4]
(c) Calculate the compressor power. [4]
(d) Calculate the rate of heat removal in the aftercooler. [4]
(e) Calculate the required mass flow rate of cooling water. [3]
(f) Comment on where the compressor work ultimately ends up. [2]
markScheme: (a) Clear sketch: CV around compressor (air in/out, power in) and aftercooler (air in/out, water in/out)
(b) SFEE Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz]; compressor Q̇ = 0; aftercooler Ẇ = 0; ΔKE, ΔPE ≈ 0; ideal gas Δh = c_pΔT
(f) Most work leaves as heat in the cooling water; remainder (≈ 5.0 kW) raises the air's enthalpy (10 K above inlet)
Correct signs and units throughout
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Draw two control volumes in series. The compressor CV: air in (state 1: 100 kPa, 300 K), air out (state 2: 450 K), shaft power in, no heat transfer. The aftercooler CV: air in (state 2), air out (state 3: 310 K), cooling water in at 15 °C and out at 25 °C, no work. (Alternatively, draw a CV round the air side only, with heat leaving to the water.)

(b) SFEE: Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h_out − h_in) + (V_out² − V_in²)/2 + g(z_out − z_in)], with heat into and work out of the CV positive. Assumptions: steady flow; ΔKE and ΔPE negligible; air is an ideal gas with constant c_p so Δh = c_pΔT; compressor adiabatic (Q̇ = 0); aftercooler does no work (Ẇ = 0) and loses no heat to the surroundings other than to the water.

(c) Compressor: −Ẇ = ṁc_p(T₂ − T₁) = 0.5 × 1.005 × 150 = 75.4 kW, so Ẇ = −75.4 kW. The negative sign shows that 75.4 kW of power must be supplied.

(d) Aftercooler air side: Q̇ = ṁc_p(T₃ − T₂) = 0.5 × 1.005 × (310 − 450) = −70.4 kW. So 70.4 kW is removed from the air.

(e) Energy balance on the water: ṁ_w c_w (25 − 15) = 70.4 kW, so ṁ_w = 70.4/(4.18 × 10) ≈ 1.68 kg/s.

(f) Of the 75.4 kW of shaft work, 70.4 kW ends up as heat in the cooling water. The remaining 5.0 kW (= 0.5 × 1.005 × 10) stays in the air as increased enthalpy, since it leaves 10 K warmer than it entered. The useful result is the air's higher pressure; an energy balance alone does not show this, which motivates the Second Law and entropy, studied in MECH0005 in Term 2.

questions.q:
A uniform ladder AB of length 5 m and weight 200 N rests with its foot A on a rough horizontal floor (μ = 0.4) and its top B against a smooth vertical wall. The ladder makes an angle of 60° with the floor. A person of weight 800 N climbs the ladder.
(a) Draw a fully labelled free body diagram of the ladder with the person at distance s from A measured along the ladder. [3]
(b) Write the three equilibrium equations. [4]
(c) Find the maximum distance s the person can climb before the ladder slips. [7]
(d) Find the normal and friction forces at A at that point. [3]
(e) Suggest two practical changes that would let the person reach the top, explaining each using your equations. [3]
markScheme: (a) FBD: N_A up, F_A towards wall at A; N_B horizontal away from wall at B; 200 N at 2.5 m along ladder; 800 N at s
(b) ΣFy: N_A = 1000 N; ΣFx: F_A = N_B; moments about A: N_B × 5 sin 60° = 200 × 2.5 cos 60° + 800 × s cos 60°
(c) Slip when F_A = μN_A = 400 N → N_B = 400 N
(d) N_A = 1000 N, F_A = 400 N (towards the wall)
(e) e.g. steeper angle (reduces moment arms ∝ cos θ, increases N_B lever arm ∝ sin θ); higher μ / anti-slip foot or footing; tie or stake foot
Correct units, convention and checks
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Forces on the ladder: at A, normal reaction N_A upwards and friction F_A horizontally towards the wall (the foot tends to slide away from the wall); at B, a horizontal normal reaction N_B pushing away from the smooth wall, with no friction; the ladder's weight of 200 N at its mid-point, 2.5 m from A along the ladder; the person's weight of 800 N at s from A along the ladder.

(b) Vertical: N_A − 200 − 800 = 0, so N_A = 1000 N.
Horizontal: F_A − N_B = 0, so F_A = N_B.
Moments about A (anticlockwise positive, wall on the right): the horizontal arm of a point s along the ladder is s cos 60° and the height of B is 5 sin 60°. N_B × 5 sin 60° − 200 × 2.5 cos 60° − 800 × s cos 60° = 0.

(c) Slipping is impending when F_A = μN_A = 0.4 × 1000 = 400 N, so N_B = 400 N. Substituting: 400 × 5 × 0.8660 = 200 × 2.5 × 0.5 + 800 × 0.5 × s, so 1732 = 250 + 400s and s = 1482/400 ≈ 3.70 m. The person can climb about 3.7 m along the 5 m ladder before it slips.

(d) At that point N_A = 1000 N upwards and F_A = 400 N towards the wall (equal to N_B).

(e) First, set the ladder steeper. The moment arms of the weights depend on cos θ and the arm of N_B on sin θ, so a steeper ladder needs a smaller N_B, and so less friction, for the same s. At 75° (a common guide is about 1 out for every 4 up), the person can reach the top. Check: N_B = (200 × 2.5 + 800 × 5) cos 75°/(5 sin 75°) ≈ 241 N < 400 N. Second, increase the available friction or restraint at the foot: an anti-slip foot (higher μ), securing the base, or someone footing the ladder adds a horizontal force or raises μN_A. Either way, the friction needed becomes less than the friction available.
